video_title: The Neuron Basis: Goodfire's Curt Tigges on Agentic Interp, Monosemanticity & Reverse Engineering
gist: Goodfire's Curt Tigges argues individual MLP neurons in Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B are far more interpretable than assumed: ~90% of activations can be ablated with minimal loss (recovered by ~100M tokens of fine-tuning), and an LLM 'neuron scientist' agent writes neuron descriptions that recover 74% of ablation damage. The neuron basis beats transcoders for MLPs and MoE experts are topically focused, but ambitious reverse engineering still requires climbing from neurons to circuits.

insights.claim: Goodfire's core thesis (with Nick Camarada) is that individual MLP neurons are far more interpretable than the field assumed: most have one main function, and polysemantic neurons carry a compact, enumerable set of meanings rather than hundreds.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Challenges the SAE-centric consensus in mechanistic interpretability; favors tooling and labs that work directly in the neuron basis.
insights.quote: It's usually not like an unbounded number of hundreds and hundreds of meanings that are just like very difficult to understand. Rather it's like a compact set of of meanings.

insights.claim: Neurons got easier to interpret because of better tools (LLM agents that comb activation examples, better circuit tracing) and because modern SwiGLU-style gated MLPs are more interpretable than older ReLU/GELU networks.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Interpretability progress is now riding frontier-model capability gains; better agents directly translate into more legible models.

insights.claim: Neuron functions are better described as verbs/control-flow gates (sending signals that make the model do something, e.g., recheck, pivot, express more or less confidence) than as nouns that merely detect concepts.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Suggests steering/monitoring at the neuron level can act on behavior directly, not just read state.
insights.quote: The neuron is doing something, right? It's not just detecting a thing. It's like sending a signal that is going to induce the model to do something else.

insights.claim: A whole class of reasoning-specific neurons controls confidence, 'wait'/recheck behavior, continuing versus pivoting approach, and error detection like off-by-one numbers, and these are steerable.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Reasoning-quality controls may be directly tunable in deployed models, a possible lever for efficiency and reliability products.

insights.claim: Monosemanticity is the wrong frame; the useful question is whether you can elucidate all the things a neuron represents, since apparent polysemanticity (clothing, exercise equipment, dishes) may be one model concept like 'things at a garage sale'.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Evaluation of interpretability tools should shift from purity metrics to complete, predictive descriptions.
insights.quote: what if the concept that the model has is things you might find at a garage sale?

insights.claim: Each SwiGLU neuron has effectively two meanings (positive and negative poles) read differently downstream, so Qwen's 5 million neurons express roughly 10 million things.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Doubles the labeling workload for full-model interpretation but keeps it bounded.

insights.claim: Dual-meaning neurons use context-switching: context pre-activates the right set of downstream readers so, e.g., an 'oral health' versus 'marine wildlife' neuron is read by fully separate reader sets.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: The gated MLP architecture functions as built-in routing logic, which helps explain why it dominates modern LLMs.

insights.claim: Facts are stored in the connections among neurons, not in single neurons, which is how 5 million neurons can encode far more than 5 million facts; a few dozen neurons encode which painters are impressionist, neo-impressionist or post-impressionist.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Knowledge editing or removal must target circuits and communities, not single units.
insights.quote: A neuron is not a fact, but the fact is in the connections between neurons.

insights.claim: Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B can have roughly 88-90% of neuron activations ablated (keeping top-64 per expert or only extreme percentiles) with performance roughly equivalent to the original on many benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Points to large potential inference savings if sparse execution can be exploited in hardware/kernels.

insights.claim: Heavy ablation actually improved ARC-AGI scores, which the guest attributes to the model becoming more confident with less internal noise distracting it from the right answer.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Suggests sparsification can act as a regularizer; worth watching for sparse-by-design model releases.
insights.quote: it doesn't have as much internally to distract itself from the right answer and the most confident thing rises to the top.

insights.claim: Sparsified models initially degrade on reasoning (looping, excessive self-checking), but about 100 million tokens of post-training, done in a single day on a few GPUs, restores performance to par or better.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Recovery is cheap relative to pre-training, lowering the cost barrier for sparse model variants.
insights.quote: Yeah, basically we were able to do it in like a single day um on a few GPUs.

insights.claim: After light fine-tuning, the sparsified model scored 5-15 points above the original on several benchmarks across math, code, MedQA and knowledge tasks, and MedQA landed within a point of the original.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Sparse models may beat dense ones on some tasks; more RL beyond 100 steps is untested upside.

insights.claim: Before fine-tuning, the sparsified model's pass@4 and pass@8 matched the original, indicating knowledge was intact and only calibration/confidence was broken.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Degradation from sparsity is a calibration problem, not knowledge loss, which is why recovery is cheap.

insights.claim: Factual recall benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, GPQA Diamond, SuperGPQA) were largely preserved under sparsity because each fact's neurons still fire when relevant; only per-token activity is pruned.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Sparse inference need not sacrifice knowledge breadth on standard benchmarks.

insights.claim: Neurons decay into noise at different activation percentiles (some meaningful down to P75, others only above P99), so per-expert top-K ablation outperforms global percentile cuts.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Practical guidance for anyone building activation-sparsity inference optimizations.

insights.claim: Story-telling needs roughly an order of magnitude fewer retained neuron firings than reasoning and coding, and the sparse model held up on coding tasks up to 32k tokens.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Task-adaptive sparsity could allow cheaper inference on creative/chat workloads than on agentic coding.

insights.claim: The host hypothesizes that weak activations may matter more over million-token contexts; the guest says this is untested beyond 32k but suspects what works at 32k extends further.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host) / Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Key open risk for sparse inference in long-context agent deployments.

insights.claim: Sparsity could produce a negative alignment tax: chips that skip zero multiplications could make sparse, more monitorable models cheaper to run.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Links interpretability to inference-cost economics, a potential tailwind for sparsity-aware hardware.

insights.claim: Goodfire's 'neuron scientist' agent clusters thousands of activating examples, forms hypotheses, runs counterfactual/steering experiments, and iterates on paragraph-length neuron descriptions against an independent predictor.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Turns interpretability into a compute-scalable process, the way agent capability now scales other research work.

insights.claim: Interpretability quality scales with applied intelligence: simple auto-interp gives vacuous labels, while stronger agents doing more work produce more predictive descriptions.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Frontier model progress compounds into interpretability; inference demand for interp workloads should grow.
insights.quote: as we apply increasing levels of intelligence then more and more of what the neuron is doing becomes legible and predictable.

insights.claim: Patching activations predicted by a separate model from the neuron description recovers 74% of the damage-weighted KL divergence lost by ablating the neuron, and binary 'does it fire here' prediction reaches the 90s.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host) / Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: A quantitative benchmark for neuron-description fidelity that can track field progress.

insights.claim: A neuron that looked uninterpretable in 50-token windows turned out to fire on the second item of a list being restated in a new format about 1,000 tokens after it was first introduced, which only agentic investigation revealed.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Many 'dead' or noisy features may be long-range structural; short-window labeling underestimates legibility.

insights.claim: Labeling cost varies widely: the most elaborate neuron-scientist run cost $45 of inference for one neuron, but a coarse pass with cheap local models (e.g., GLM 5.3) plus selective deep dives on hard neurons makes full-model interpretation affordable.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: At millions of neurons, cost-tiered pipelines matter; open local models are a cheap substrate for interp at scale.
insights.quote: The most expensive one took $45 of inference for a single neuron which is pretty crazy.

insights.claim: The same agentic tool-use approach could equally be applied to SAE features, making it an innovation regardless of which basis is used.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: The method is portable across interpretability stacks.

insights.claim: Substituting a transcoder for the MLP incurs more loss than simply keeping the top-K neurons, and transcoder features largely recapitulate neurons or sparse neuron combinations, so for MLPs the neuron basis should be preferred.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the need for expensive dictionary-learning helper models for MLP analysis.
insights.quote: you have more loss if you substitute a transcoder for the MLP than if you just use the top K neurons instead, which really suggests that you should be looking more at the neurons.

insights.claim: SAEs remain useful mainly for the residual stream, which has genuine superposition and complex geometry; understanding residual stream geometry is a major prerequisite for ambitious reverse engineering.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Residual stream analysis is the next bottleneck and research frontier.

insights.claim: Mixture-of-experts experts in Qwen are concentrated on roughly one to three topics each (algebra, geometry, timekeeping, legal/constitutional text, medical subtopics), contrary to the earlier view that experts are uninterpretable.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Expert specialization enables targeted capability removal or monitoring in MoE models.

insights.claim: Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B has 40 layers, each with 256 experts of 512 neurons (~130,000 neurons per layer, ~5 million total), with 8 experts active per layer, plus gated DeltaNet in three-quarters of attention layers, features shared with frontier open-source models.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Qwen serves as a representative proxy for frontier open-weight architectures in interp research.

insights.claim: SwiGLU's 'double negative' activations (gate and up projections both negative) are poorly understood; ReGLU models like Gemma 4 avoid them by design, and Kimi K3 neurons rarely use them.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Architecture choices may differ materially in interpretability; an open research question.

insights.claim: Monitoring is the first practical application: an outside researcher found a single neuron that fires on reward-hacking text, though it may cover only a subtype of reward hacking.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Cheap neuron-level monitors are near-term deployable safety products, but coverage gaps are a risk.

insights.claim: Neuron-based persona creation and steering is surprisingly practical, because many neurons affect how the model responds and its personality.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Opens a product path for fine-grained model personality control without retraining.

insights.claim: Because existing models are already fairly interpretable, the industry may need a smaller alignment tax, meaning less need for expensive interpretability-specific architectures, while sparsity and localization of knowledge would still help.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Reduces the expected cost of safety compliance for model developers.
insights.quote: maybe we need less of that create an interpretability specific architecture that is expensive to on than we thought because maybe we can just interpret the existing ones.

insights.claim: Training models to localize dangerous knowledge (e.g., bio/WMD) into specific experts or neurons, as gradient-routing-style work proposes, would let developers ablate it before public release.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: A path to releasing open-weight models with surgically removed hazardous capabilities.

insights.claim: The host cites Jensen Huang saying only 10-20% of resources go into making a product and 80-90% into making it safe and reliable, arguing AI labs should spend far more compute on monitoring and interpretability.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: If adopted, safety/monitoring compute becomes a large new source of GPU demand.

insights.claim: A full list of neuron descriptions is not a reverse-engineered model; understanding requires climbing a tree of abstractions from neurons to subcircuits, neuron communities and super-circuits, analogous to physics, chemistry and biology.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Interpretability is not 'solved'; expect years of work before behavior-level guarantees.

insights.claim: Progress will come from two ends converging: bottom-up neuron/circuit cataloging and top-down steering vectors and training effects, until researchers can see what changes when a model becomes reward-hacking, eval-aware or more cooperative.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Signals the research roadmap for interpretability labs like Goodfire.

insights.claim: A neuron-basis analogue of Anthropic-style 'tracing the thoughts' work is achievable soon; models can already reconstruct a paragraph's entities and relationships from its attribution graph and firing neurons, relevant to reading hidden thought in neuralese or KV-cache communication.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Could underpin monitoring of models that reason in latent space, a growing safety concern.

insights.claim: Researchers can replicate neuron interpretation on small local models today, and Goodfire plans to release neuron labels; the work builds on prior neuron-interp by Transluce.
insights.speaker: Curt Tigges (Goodfire)
insights.so_what: Low barrier to entry broadens the interp ecosystem.
